fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Better the Devil You Know", "body": "Dylan Saccoccio takes the episode title from an NRO mission patch whose Latin motto reads better the devil you know, and argues that the system holds people through familiarity: it reaches you through your parents, their parents, your priests and your community, so questioning it means ostracising yourself. Continuing part two of their work on Reverend Robert Taylor's astronomical theological lectures, the pair set that beside Godfrey Higgins's line that the devil is the grand ally of priests, certainly no devil, no priests, and read Taylor, jailed for blasphemy, turning the charge of blasphemy back on his accusers."}, {"title": "Job, Yove and the Name of Apollo", "body": "Dylan traces the name Job back through the Targums to a Hebrew form he transliterates as aiub or aiuv, noting that the beit serves as both b and v and that the vowel points arrived late, so reconstructing a dead language is, in his words, all guesswork and all opinion based. He links yove to Yova, Jehovah, Jupiter and the first father, Ju-pater, and says the same root in its aub or ob form signifies a serpent, a ghost and a necromancer. Citing Jacob Bryant, he argues the very name of Apollo is the name of Yove."}, {"title": "Abadir, Abaddon and the Two Halves of Job", "body": "Working from a Jacob Bryant passage on the oracles of Apollo, Chance Garton picks up the pillar name Abadir as a compound of ab and adir, then applies rotacism, swapping the final r for an n, to arrive at Abaddon, the angel of the bottomless pit covered in the previous episode. He reads the poem as astrological allegory, with Jehovah and the devil as two halves of one character, the devil and the angel on each shoulder, and warns that teaching it as literal history leaves children believing that being too good makes you a target."}, {"title": "Ventriloquist Oracles and the Degrees of the Priesthood", "body": "Dylan cites a lexicon admitting that the root meaning of aub can only be remotely conjectured and that its distinction from idoni is unknown. He suggests the Pythian oracles and serpent cults worked partly by ventriloquism, a priest throwing his voice through a statue, and reads Moses as a title for an initiate who forbids the Israelites from consulting ob and idoni. He sets out a degree ladder of Christians as good fellows, Jews as men of God, Israelites as men of Chronos, then Hebrews, obri, those who passed over, tying idoni to the Greek gnostes and to Adonai and Adonis."}, {"title": "Buried Compasses and the Bite of a Mad Parson", "body": "Chance reads Taylor's claim that the polyglot Bible's own margin dates Job to about 1520 BC among the Midianites, making it the oldest book either the Jewish or the Christian world receives as inspired. Taylor further contends the priests knew the magnetic needle long before Marco Polo, carrying the magnet in a compass box as the ark of the covenant, and hid it under allegories like Hercules sailing in a vase directed by the arrow of Apollo. Dylan closes on kion, dog in Greek and priest in Hebrew, and on dog reversed as god."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: The Book of Job is one of the oldest texts in the Old Testament, and one of the most studied. It's also where the figure of the devil first appears in scripture. Robert Taylor, the 19th century clergyman known for his astro-theological lectures, spent years tracing the symbolism of the devil through the Bible and the ancient world.
fields.Intro Paragraph 2: In Inner Whirled 7, Chance and co-host Dylan Saccoccio continue working through Taylor's research, picking up from where the previous devil episode left off.

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Revelation 12 and Genesis as a Star Map", "body": "Chance walks through Revelation chapter twelve and Genesis line by line, swapping King James mistranslations for the Greek and Hebrew astronomy underneath them. The woman clothed in the sun becomes Virgo, her child becomes Leo by way of the Babylonian word Charu for both infant and king, and the red dragon becomes Hydra or Scorpio swallowing stars below the horizon. In Genesis, Jehovah plays Hercules the storm god, Adam and Eve are Bootes and Virgo, and the serpent is Hydra, with the very order God expels them from Eden matching the order the constellations sink below the western horizon each night."}, {"title": "The Serpent as Healer, Watcher and Devil", "body": "The serpent keeps returning as one symbol wearing many masks across the exclusive material. It is the devil in the garden, the Holy Ghost's cloven tongue at Pentecost, and the brazen serpent Moses raises on a pole so the same creature that stings also heals. It is also the Eye of Providence, since the Hebrew word for serpent doubles as the word for watching and divining. Dylan traces the image further into the eye on a penis, the almond shaped vulva, and the ouroboros circling winter's dead months, arguing every culture's watching, healing or destroying spirit is this one astronomical serpent renamed."}, {"title": "One God Under a Hundred Names", "body": "Dylan builds a chain of letter swaps arguing Job, Iov, Jove, Jehovah, Jupiter, Deva and Zeus are one word worn down by different alphabets. Reading Godfrey Higgins at length, he shows Krishna born in the house of Vasudeva, the Etruscan Jupiter Tinia, and the Chinese Yao all reducing to the same root, concluding language itself, not history, invented the appearance of many separate gods. Chance backs this with his own research into Bacchus and Eve, arguing the Targum's serpent name Huia is simply Eve with her letters swapped, making Eve herself a forgotten title of Bacchus."}, {"title": "Taylor's Case That God and the Devil Are One", "body": "The whole exclusive block builds toward Reverend Taylor's own conclusion, read aloud near the end, that paganism and Christianity are the same religion, and that God, devil, Christ, Satan, angel and demon are all names for one being who made both day and night. Chance and Dylan treat this as the payoff of their entire etymological project, arguing the priesthood deliberately disguised a single astronomical system behind translated names so only initiates could see through it, while ordinary believers were kept fighting over religions that were never actually different from one another."}, {"title": "Job's Story Rewritten as Astronomy", "body": "Returning to the book of Job itself, the hosts retranslate its opening scenes, arguing Satan is simply one of the sons of God, meaning the stars, standing before Jehovah rather than opposing him. They read Job's calamities as astronomical events in disguise, with the Sabians who destroy his servants actually rendering Shiva the destroyer in the Hebrew, and Job nine nine's bear reinterpreted as a moth linked to soul and psyche. The chapter closes by tying Moses's healing serpent staff, the plague of fiery seraphim in Numbers, and Isis's serpent Ti into the same solar mythology running through the book."}]
